title: Born Bent
speaker: Elijah Stanley
card_summary: Elijah Stanley follows David’s confession in Psalm 51:3–5 from the collapse of self-defense, through the way tolerated compromise formed David’s later fall, to sin’s deepest character as rebellion against God and its reach into human nature. The sermon then turns to Jesus as the greater David: the sinless King bears judgment, creates clean hearts, preserves his people, and calls guilty sinners out of hiding into grace.
section_intro: The sermon begins at 00:38 after opening non-sermon audio. Elijah uses social-media curation and a deceptively advertised dining table to expose the instinct to manage appearances, then reads Psalm 51:3–5. The resulting outline preserves his chronological movement from confession, through David’s earlier compromises and the doctrine of sin, to the cross, new birth, kingdom hope, invitation, and closing prayer.

ledger_caption: 55 confirmed Scripture units, in sermon order

movements.heading: The instinct to manage the image
bullets: Elijah opens with the contrast between polished presentation and actual defects: people curate explanations for bad days, idealized social-media lives, and Marketplace listings that conceal what is broken.
The humor establishes the sermon’s diagnosis: people instinctively lead with the version of the truth that makes them look best rather than with their defects.

children.heading: Image management in an age of curation
bullets: Social media makes every marriage, vacation, child, workout, and coffee look flourishing; the Marketplace dining-table illustration exposes how descriptions are designed to make defects easy to overlook.
Elijah turns the observation toward the congregation: this is not merely an online habit but a human instinct to curate an image, manage reputation, and spin the story in one’s favor.

children.heading: Spiritual public relations: renaming and hiding sin
bullets: People soften guilt by saying they misspoke rather than lied, shared concern rather than gossiped, or were passionate rather than lost their temper.
Christians can confess without a guilty person in the sentence; minimization, redirection, comparison, blame, secrecy, and respectable spiritual language become damage control.
The need to believe ourselves good makes excuses feel safer than honest confession.

children.heading: David runs out of excuses before God
bullets: Elijah connects to Pastor Josh’s prior message: Psalm 51 shows David after Nathan’s confrontation has stripped away his management of the Bathsheba scandal.
Exposure is frightening but merciful; the more dangerous place is remaining convinced that there is nothing to confess.
He reads Psalm 51:3–5 as the controlling text: David knows his transgressions, names his evil before God, vindicates God’s judgment, and admits sin reaches back to conception.

children.heading: Opening prayer for receptive hearts
bullets: Elijah asks God to open hearts, minds, and eyes through the difficult written Word and thanks him for grace and mercy toward sinners.

movements.heading: Confession begins when the sinner agrees with God
bullets: Elijah slows down over David’s words, ‘I know my transgressions,’ and defines repentance as the end of self-defense.

children.heading: Repentance begins by agreeing with God’s verdict
bullets: David is not vaguely acknowledging that mistakes were made or that others were offended; he names his own transgressions without softening them.
Repentance begins when the sinner stops arguing, negotiating, or presenting evidence for the defense and says, ‘Lord, you are right about me.’

children.heading: Confession tells God nothing new
bullets: God already saw the deed, heard the words, and knew the motive, desire, fear, and intended gain underneath the action.
Confession is agreement: when God calls the act sin and evil and the person guilty, repentance answers yes rather than appealing the verdict.

children.heading: The catastrophe had a history
bullets: Elijah returns to the historical setting of Psalm 51: David’s adultery, manipulation of Uriah, and arranged death did not erupt from nowhere.
Sin usually begins before the visible catastrophe—in governable desires, moved boundaries, small disobediences, and compromises whose delayed consequences make them look safe.

movements.heading: Tolerated compromise forms the person who later falls
bullets: Elijah traces earlier warning signs in David to show that hidden patterns train desires and prepare later ruin.

children.heading: Nabal exposes David’s wounded pride and violent anger
bullets: In 1 Samuel 25, Nabal’s contempt provokes David to arm his men and set out to kill every male in the household, despite David’s earlier restraint toward Saul.
The contrast shows that self-control in one area can coexist with corruption in another: David spared Saul under pressure but nearly shed innocent blood when his pride was wounded.
Abigail warns that needless bloodshed and personal vengeance would burden David’s conscience; David recognizes that God sent her and praises her judgment for restraining him.

children.heading: Prevention of the act did not remove the sinful impulse
bullets: God’s providence stopped the slaughter, but David’s rage, pride, and willingness to use force against an offender had already been revealed and still required confrontation.
After Nabal’s death David marries Abigail, while the text also identifies Ahinoam of Jezreel as another wife.

children.heading: Polygamy becomes normalized rebellion
bullets: Second Samuel 3:2–5 lists six sons by six women during David’s reign in Hebron; Elijah treats this as evidence of what kind of king David was becoming, not incidental family data.
Deuteronomy’s law forbade Israel’s king to multiply wives lest his heart turn away. David’s exception became a habit, the habit became normal, and the normal became invisible.
Tolerated sin dulls the conscience incrementally: it screams at the first crossing, then speaks, then whispers, and eventually is no longer heard.

children.heading: The Bathsheba account reveals desire trained to take
bullets: Second Samuel 11 places David in Jerusalem while his men fight. Seeing Bathsheba may begin unintentionally, but inquiry continues after servants identify her family and her husband Uriah, one of David’s loyal mighty men.
Years of indulged appetite have taught David that desire is sufficient reason to take: he sees, asks, receives a warning, and takes.
Pregnancy makes the supposedly controlled sin control David. Lust demands deception, failed manipulation demands murder, and Uriah carries his own death order back to battle.
David’s later marriage to the widow can be presented as royal compassion, but the managed public story cannot alter the Lord’s verdict that David’s deed displeased him.

children.heading: Kill sin before it matures
bullets: Elijah states the principle: the sin one makes peace with today can become the sin that masters tomorrow; the useful question is where present compromises are leading.

Private choices form desires. Kept boundaries strengthen the next boundary, while moved boundaries make later movement easier; affairs begin with messages, hidden conversations, repeated looks, and welcomed attention.
Quoting John Owen, Elijah urges believers to be killing sin rather than accommodating, renaming, negotiating with, or keeping it publicly manageable.
James describes desire’s progression through temptation and conception to mature sin and death; therefore the church must evaluate not only a compromise’s small beginning but its end.

Application: identify the small compromise, moved boundary, dismissed conviction, or fed appetite; bring it to the Lord and to those harmed, trusting God’s promise to forgive and purify confessing sinners.

movements.heading: Every horizontal sin is first rebellion against God
bullets: David has injured many people, yet Psalm 51 looks upward because the deepest character of sin is revolt against God’s rule.

children.heading: Vertical guilt does not erase horizontal accountability
bullets: David sinned against Bathsheba, Uriah, his family, manipulated soldiers, and the nation, yet confesses, ‘Against you, you only have I sinned.’

Elijah insists that David is magnifying the divine offense, not denying human victims. Confession to God never exempts a person from making matters right with a spouse, child, church, or other wounded person.
Wanting Psalm 51’s cleansing without Matthew 5’s reconciliation misuses mercy as protection from an awkward but necessary confession.
Sin against another person is first sin against the God whose image that person bears.

children.heading: Sin is cosmic treason rooted in Eden
bullets: Sin is not merely breaking an impersonal rule; it is the creature telling the Creator, ‘You made me, but you will not rule me,’ and attempting to become its own authority.
The serpent’s offer was not merely forbidden food but autonomy—to be like God and define good and evil independently. Every later sin repeats that Edenic reach.

Romans 8 calls the flesh-governed mind hostile to God and unable to submit to God’s law. Apart from Christ’s saving grace and the Spirit’s work, the natural heart wants God’s gifts without his government.
Because all things are from, through, and for God, he claims every area of life rather than serving as a personal consultant.

children.heading: The offense is measured by the worth of the one offended
bullets: Elijah argues that the seriousness of an offense rises with the dignity and authority of the one offended: killing an insect, striking a person, and attacking a judge or law-enforcement officer are not treated as morally identical acts.
Because sin is committed against the infinitely worthy Creator, its gravity cannot be measured only by the visible size of the act or its immediate human consequences.
The rebellion is also irrational dependence: sinners borrow breath, heartbeat, strength, and life from God while using those gifts to resist his rule.

children.heading: All sin is committed before the face of God
bullets: David’s words ‘evil in your sight’ overturn the illusion that authority, darkness, privacy, deleted messages, hidden accounts, concealed motives, or religious language can cover sin from God.
Elijah names this coram Deo—life before God’s face—and recalls Hebrews 4:13: creation is uncovered before the one to whom all must give account.
God sees not only actions and words but the pride, praise-hunger, cowardice, and mixed motives hidden beneath apparently righteous conduct.

children.heading: Repentance stops putting God on trial
bullets: The secret place reveals not who one is when nobody sees, but who one is when only God sees; therefore David’s confession must become the believer’s own.
David accepts that God’s verdict and judgment are right. Genuine repentance does not ask God to lower the standard or appeal the sentence; it vindicates God rather than defending self.

movements.heading: God’s wrath is the righteous verdict sinners deserve
bullets: Elijah argues that God’s judgment seems excessive only where human sin and divine holiness have been minimized.

children.heading: A culture of self-esteem puts God’s holiness on trial
bullets: Modern culture teaches basic human goodness, entitlement to happiness, and the unthinkability of deserved judgment; some Christians then act as God’s public-relations department and soften his words.
True repentance reverses the courtroom: God is not the defendant who must explain himself; the sinner is.

children.heading: Wrath is already being revealed against sin
bullets: Romans 1:18 presents God’s wrath as presently revealed against godlessness, wickedness, and truth suppression.
Funerals, broken families, wars, and graveyards witness that sin’s curse has fallen. Death is not natural but the wages of sin.

children.heading: Holy wrath makes Calvary necessary
bullets: God’s wrath is not love’s opposite but holy opposition to what destroys what he loves, analogous to righteous anger at trafficking or harm to a child.
Divine wrath is settled, perfect justice rather than uncontrolled rage; Scripture, Jesus, and the apostles do not apologize for it.

Without real wrath, Calvary is a tragic misunderstanding. With it, Christ dies not merely to inspire but to drink the judgment sinners deserved; Elijah transitions with the hymn line that the wrath of God was satisfied in Christ’s death.

movements.heading: Born bent: sin reaches into human nature
bullets: Returning to Psalm 51:5, Elijah moves from David’s guilty acts to the sinful nature from which they came.

children.heading: Psalm 51:5 and the untrained selfishness of a child
bullets: Elijah reads David’s confession that he was sinful from birth and conception, then anticipates the objection that babies appear innocent.
His eight-month-old daughter’s beauty and untrained demands illustrate the distinction: she is not wicked like an unrepentant adult, but already has the inward-curved heart shared by everyone.
Parents celebrate milestones but not a first lie; generosity, truthfulness, gratitude, and obedience require teaching, while selfishness, lying, complaint, and rebellion appear naturally.

children.heading: The problem is a nature, not merely isolated acts
bullets: David’s problem did not begin on Bathsheba’s roof, with kingship, or at Samuel’s anointing; it goes down to his nature.
Elijah defines total depravity not as being maximally evil but as sin touching every faculty—mind, desire, affection, will, and conscience: ‘I sin because I am a sinner.’
Changing environment, city, job, spouse, income, apps, therapy, or house cannot remove the common denominator: the self. Psalm 51 contradicts the claim that people are basically good.

The poison-drop illustration preserves both truths: fallen people still bear God’s image and can display kindness, beauty, creativity, courage, and love, yet every faculty and even righteous pursuits can be stained by mixed motives.

children.heading: A bent heart needs new birth, not a tune-up
bullets: Hearts drift naturally away from God; people accidentally become worldly, not holy, disciplined in prayer, or Christlike. Elijah echoes J. C. Ryle’s image of a stone naturally moving downward.
Better habits and surroundings cannot supply the needed new heart. Ezekiel promised a heart of flesh in place of stone, and Jesus demanded new birth—not improvement, reform, or polish.
Because dead people cannot raise themselves, Christianity is not behavior modification but God’s act of making the spiritually dead alive and new by the Holy Spirit.
If the deepest problem is nature rather than merely record, only the God who formed the heart can create the clean heart David seeks.

movements.heading: The greater David answers guilt at the cross
bullets: Elijah turns from humanity’s inability to God’s work through Jesus, the king who stands where David fell.

children.heading: Where David failed, Christ prevailed
bullets: David stole another man’s bride; Jesus gave himself for his bride. David killed an innocent man to cover his own sin; Jesus was killed by guilty people to cover theirs.
David deserved judgment and pleaded for mercy; Jesus deserved glory and willingly took the place of those under judgment.
Everything David failed to be Christ became, everything David deserved Christ bore, and everything David longed for Christ secured.

children.heading: Justice and mercy meet for guilty people
bullets: God’s holy wrath was neither ignored nor explained away but poured out on the sinless Son. At Calvary sin is punished and sinners are forgiven without conflict between justice and mercy.
The gospel does not save good people—there are none—but guilty rebels, adulterers, liars, idolaters, and the proud, including people like David, Elijah, and the congregation.

Repentance does not earn favor; Christ has earned what sinners could not. The crushed are not beyond mercy, and the self-confident must compare themselves to Christ’s spotless holiness rather than to neighbors or notorious sinners.

children.heading: The prayer for a clean heart becomes gospel hope
bullets: Elijah reads Psalm 51:10–12: create a pure heart, renew a steadfast spirit, preserve God’s presence and Spirit, and restore salvation’s joy with a willing spirit.
The needed answer is new creation rather than a tune-up. Christ lived the life sinners could not, died the death they deserved, and rose so that those who repent and believe may become new.

movements.heading: The reigning Christ makes sinners new and advances his kingdom
bullets: The greater David reigns on an everlasting throne and actively calls, renews, preserves, and gathers his people.

children.heading: The Shepherd regenerates and keeps his people
bullets: The sinless King is not anxiously hoping sinners find home; he calls the dead, replaces stone hearts with flesh, and his sheep hear his voice.
He rescues rebels, adopts enemies, justifies the guilty, sanctifies his people, and will lose none whom the Father has given him.

children.heading: Christ’s kingdom, gospel, and church will not fail
bullets: Christ has conquered sin, death, and hell, and the kingdoms of the world belong to him.
The gospel will accomplish the purpose for which it was sent rather than limp over the finish line.
The gates of hell will not prevail against Christ’s church but will crumble as the King advances.

children.heading: Come into the light because grace is greater
bullets: Elijah calls the church to stop hiding, minimizing, blaming, and bargaining; confess sin and rely on Jesus’ mercy rather than personal resolve.
No sinner, conscience, or hard heart is beyond Christ’s cleansing, forgiveness, and grace, because where sin increased grace abounded more.
The Christ who restored David and raised Lazarus still forgives and raises the spiritually dead; his reign guarantees the coming worldwide knowledge of the Lord’s glory.
The final appeal is to come because Christ is worthy, not because the sinner is.

movements.heading: Closing prayer: create in us a clean heart
bullets: Elijah thanks God for everlasting mercy and love toward sinners and asks that the church know and be known by him.
He prays Psalm 51’s request for a clean heart, renewed spirit, and sustaining power, then asks for grace, faithfulness, mercy, and honest inward reflection.

Recognizing sin’s weight makes Calvary more beautiful; Elijah asks God to remove contrary desires, thoughts, words, and deeds so that all of life is for God’s glory, and to strengthen the church by the Holy Spirit.
